html:
The second Arab siege of Constantinople, in 717 and 718, was the last and largest attempt by the Umayyad Caliphate to take the Byzantine capital. It came after twenty years of Arab gains in Anatolia, while the empire was weakened by the Twenty Years' Anarchy.

The army, led by the caliph's brother Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, crossed into Thrace in the summer of 717 and dug in before the land walls, while a great fleet tried to cut the city off by sea. The new emperor Leo III had stocked the city well. Greek fire burned part of the Arab fleet, and the walls held.

The winter was very hard and the besiegers starved. Supply fleets sent in spring were destroyed after their Christian crews deserted, and the Bulgars attacked the Arab camp. In August 718 the siege was called off, and many ships were lost to storms on the way home.

The failure ended Arab hopes of taking the city and fixed the Byzantine-Arab border in Anatolia for centuries. Some historians rank it with the Battle of Tours as a check on Muslim expansion into Europe.
